questions.q: What is the literary term for a poem that draws directly on the poet's personal life, family history, and emotional conflicts, often using a first-person speaker who closely resembles the poet?
questions.a: The term is **confessional poetry**. A wrong answer (e.g., "autobiographical poetry," "narrative poetry," or "lyric poetry") reveals that the student conflates generic categories: all confessional poetry is autobiographical, but not all autobiographical poetry is confessional — the latter implies a raw, unmediated exposure of private trauma, taboo subjects (female sexuality, mental illness, family dysfunction), and a deliberate blurring of poet and speaker. Kamala Das is a foundational figure in Indian English confessional poetry; missing this label means missing the poem's radical honesty about a woman's ambivalence toward her own heritage.

questions.q: In the poem, the great-grandmother claims "we had the oldest blood / My brother and she and I / The oldest blood in the world / A blood thin and clear and fine" while contrasting it with the blood of "the always poor" and "the new-rich men" which is "thick as gruel / And muddy as a ditch." Explain what this blood metaphor reveals about the great-grandmother's worldview and the social structure she represents.
questions.a: The metaphor reveals a **feudal, caste-inflected aristocratic worldview** that equates lineage with biological superiority. "Thin and clear and fine" blood signifies refinement, purity, and ancient privilege — the great-grandmother's Nair aristocratic self-fashioning. "Thick as gruel / And muddy as a ditch" dehumanizes the poor and the newly wealthy as biologically inferior. A wrong answer that treats this as merely "the grandmother's pride in her family" misses the **systemic violence** of the metaphor: it naturalizes class/caste hierarchy by making it somatic. The poem later interrogates this when the speaker — who shares that "oldest blood" — abandons the house, fails to grow rich, and hears the house's death rattle from afar. The metaphor is not endorsed; it is staged for critique.

questions.q: The poem shifts between three time frames: (a) the speaker's childhood with her brother and great-grandmother, (b) the great-grandmother's youth (elephant rides, marriage, early widowhood), and (c) the speaker's adulthood after the great-grandmother's death. Identify the stanza where each time frame dominates, and explain how the shifts are signaled without explicit temporal markers like "years later."
questions.a: Time frame (a) dominates the opening stanzas ("When we were children / My brother and I..."). Time frame (b) takes over when the great-grandmother narrates her past ("She told us how she rode her elephant / When she was ten or eleven..."). Time frame (c) begins at "Finally she lay dying / In her eighty sixth year..." and continues to the end. Shifts are signaled by **change in verb tense** (present/past habitual → past narrative → present reflective), **shift in agency** (great-grandmother as storyteller → great-grandmother as dying woman → speaker as guilty survivor), and **spatial relocation** (house as playground → house as decaying body → house as haunted memory heard "From every town I live in"). A student who cannot map these shifts will read the poem as a flat sequence of memories rather than a layered meditation on how past inhabits present.

questions.q: Compare the great-grandmother's relationship to the house ("For I love this house, it hurts me much / To watch it die") with the speaker's adult relationship to it ("I have let you down / Old house, I seek forgiveness... I have plucked your soul / Like a pip from a fruit / And have flung it into your pyre"). What does this contrast reveal about the poem's attitude toward **filial duty** and **female agency**?
questions.a: The great-grandmother's love is **embodied, sacrificial, and static** — she identifies entirely with the house, feeds on "God" (tradition), and dies weeping for its decay. The speaker's relationship is **guilty, active, and mobile** — she promises reconstruction, fails, leaves, and later performs a violent metaphoric separation ("plucked your soul / Like a pip from a fruit"). This contrast reveals that **filial duty in a patriarchal-feudal system demands women's self-erasure** (the great-grandmother's "feasts were monotonous / For the only dish was always God"), while **female agency requires a rupture that feels like betrayal**. The poem refuses to resolve this: the speaker calls herself "callous" and "selfish" but insists "do not blame my blood" — agency is won at the cost of internalized misogyny. A student who sees only "ungrateful granddaughter" misses the poem's feminist critique of the very structure that makes the great-grandmother's devotion the only available script for women.

questions.q: The poem ends with the speaker hearing the house's death sounds "From every town I live in" and listing what her blood remembers: "All the gems and all the gold / And all the perfumes and the oils / And the stately / Elephant ride..." Evaluate whether this ending represents **closure** or **perpetual haunting**. Support your judgment with evidence from the poem's structure and imagery.
questions.a: It is **perpetual haunting**, not closure. Evidence: (1) The present-tense "I know the rats are running now / Across the darkened halls" — the house's decay continues in real time, parallel to the speaker's life. (2) The auditory hallucination ("I hear the rattle of its death / The noise of rafters creaking / And the windows' whine") follows her geographically ("From every town I live in") — distance does not mute it. (3) The final image — blood remembering "gems," "gold," "perfumes," "elephant ride" — is a **catalog of feudal luxury**, not emotional reconciliation. The blood remembers privilege, not the great-grandmother's pain or the speaker's guilt. (4) The poem's last word is "ride..." — an ellipsis, not a period. The ride continues. A student arguing for "closure" because the speaker "seeks forgiveness" confuses a ritual gesture with resolution; the poem's form (enjambment, recurring present tense, unresolved final image) enacts the impossibility of closure.

questions.q: Write a four-line stanza in free verse that could serve as a **prequel** to "Blood" — spoken by the great-grandmother on her elephant ride to the Siva shrine — using at least two images from the poem (e.g., "sandal for her breasts," "jewel box," "brocade from the north") and revealing her inner thought that the poem only hints at.
questions.a:
A strong answer will: (1) adopt the great-grandmother's voice — proud, sensory, perhaps secretly afraid; (2) incorporate two poem images organically; (3) reveal a hidden thought (e.g., fear of widowhood, awareness of performing a role, doubt about "oldest blood"); (4) use free verse — no forced rhyme, rhythm shaped by breath. Example:
> The sandal paste cools my breasts, the brocade weighs heavy —
> Ten years old and already the jewel box knows my fingers.
> The elephant sways; the Siva shrine waits.
> *Does the god see the widow inside the bride?*
A weak answer will mimic the poem's language without a distinct voice, force a rhyme scheme, or state the obvious ("I am happy riding my elephant") — revealing the student cannot inhabit a perspective other than the speaker's.
